# STM32H743 AIO Nano FC + 4-in-1 ESC: Power-Stage and DShot Timer Architecture (Job #48)

## 0. Architectural Clarifications and Assumptions

**Partitioning.** On every production AIO design, the STM32H743 runs ArduPilot only. Each ESC channel's 48 kHz commutation PWM is generated by a dedicated ESC MCU (AT32F421 or STM32G071) running AM32 or BLHeli_32. The H743 never generates the 48 kHz bridge PWM. Its job is DShot600 output and eRPM telemetry capture.

**Baseline assumptions.** Replace these with your vendor's datasheet values. Every equation below is parametric, so you can re-run it with real numbers.

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bus voltage (6S full) | V_bus | 25.2 V | Worst case for switching loss |
| Burst phase current per ESC | I_pk | 80 A | Requirement |
| MOSFET | — | 40 V, DFN3.3×3.3 class | Typical nano 4-in-1 |
| R_DS(on) @ 25 °C, V_GS = 10 V | R₂₅ | 1.5 mΩ | Typical |
| R_DS(on) tempco @ T_j = 100 °C | k_T | ×1.45 | Typical trench MOSFET |
| Gate charge / Miller charge | Q_g / Q_gd | 40 nC / 8 nC | Typical |
| Effective transition time | t_r + t_f | 30 ns | ~1 A gate drive into Q_gd |
| Dead time | t_dt | 100 ns | AM32-class default region |
| Body diode V_F / Q_rr | — | 0.8 V / 40 nC | Typical |
| PWM frequency | f_sw | 48 kHz | Requirement |
| Board | — | 30.5 × 30.5 mm, 6 L, 2 oz | Nano AIO class |

## 1. Conduction-Loss Model (80 A Burst)

### 1.1 Current paths

The bridge runs 6-step trapezoidal commutation with complementary (synchronous) PWM. At any instant, one phase leg is PWM-switching and another leg has its low-side FET held ON.

- During the ON interval, current flows through Q_H (PWM leg) and Q_L (return leg).
- During the OFF interval, current flows through Q_L' (PWM leg, synchronous rectification) and Q_L (return leg).

So the current always flows through exactly **two** conducting channels, regardless of duty cycle:

$$P_{cond,ch} = I_{rms}^2 \cdot 2R_{DS(on)}(T_j)$$

### 1.2 Temperature-corrected R_DS(on)

$$R_{DS(on)}(T_j) = R_{25}\left[1 + \alpha (T_j - 25)\right],\quad \alpha \approx 0.006\,/^\circ\text{C}$$

$$R(100^\circ C) = 1.5 \times 1.45 = 2.18\ \text{m}\Omega$$

### 1.3 Ripple correction

The phase inductance L_ph adds triangular ripple to the current:

$$\Delta I = \frac{(V_{bus} - V_{bemf})\, D}{L_{ph}\, f_{sw}},\qquad I_{rms}^2 = I_{pk}^2 + \frac{\Delta I^2}{12}$$

Take a typical 5-inch motor with L_ph ≈ 15 µH (line-to-line, so 2 × 7.5 µH), D = 0.5, and V_bus − V_bemf ≈ 10 V at full load:

$$\Delta I = \frac{10 \times 0.5}{15\,\mu\text{H} \times 48\,\text{kHz}} \approx 6.9\ \text{A} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\Delta I^2}{12} \approx 4\ \text{A}^2$$

This is negligible against 6400 A².

### 1.4 Result

$$P_{cond,ch} = 80^2 \times 2 \times 2.18\,\text{m}\Omega = \mathbf{27.9\ W\ per\ ESC\ channel}$$

### 1.5 Copper and sense losses

These are not negligible at 80 A.

| Element | Resistance | Loss @ 80 A |
|---|---|---|
| Shunt (shared bus, 0.25 mΩ, sees I_bus, not I_ph) | 0.25 mΩ | see note |
| Phase pad + trace (2 oz, 6 mm × 3 mm, two layers paralleled) | ~0.15 mΩ | 0.96 W |
| Bus planes per channel share | ~0.10 mΩ | 0.64 W |

Note on the shunt: at 4 × 80 A × D ≈ 160 A average bus current, the shunt dissipates 160² × 0.25 mΩ = **6.4 W**. That is a hotspot, so use a 2512 or 3920 metal-strip resistor or a Hall sensor.

## 2. Switching-Loss Model at 48 kHz

Only the PWM-ing leg switches hard. Each term below is computed per channel.

### 2.1 V–I overlap (hard-switched high-side)

$$P_{VI} = \tfrac12 V_{bus} I (t_r + t_f) f_{sw} = \tfrac12 (25.2)(80)(30\,\text{ns})(48\,\text{kHz}) = \mathbf{1.45\ W}$$

The effective transition time is driven by the Miller plateau:

$$t_{r,f} \approx \frac{Q_{gd}}{I_g},\qquad I_g = \frac{V_{drv} - V_{plateau}}{R_{g,ext} + R_{g,int}} \approx \frac{10 - 3.5}{4.7 + 1.5} \approx 1.05\ \text{A} \Rightarrow t \approx 7.6\ \text{ns (ideal)}$$

Commutation-loop inductance roughly doubles this in practice, which is why 15 ns per edge is used in the 30 ns budget.

### 2.2 Dead-time body-diode conduction

$$P_{dt} = V_F \cdot I \cdot 2 t_{dt} \cdot f_{sw} = 0.8 \times 80 \times 200\,\text{ns} \times 48\,\text{kHz} = \mathbf{0.61\ W}$$

### 2.3 Reverse recovery

$$P_{rr} = V_{bus} Q_{rr} f_{sw} = 25.2 \times 40\,\text{nC} \times 48\,\text{kHz} = \mathbf{0.048\ W}$$

Q_rr increases with di/dt and temperature, so derate ×2 for the worst case, giving about 0.1 W.
